stages.name: Comparative advantage: diagrams, specialisation and limits
stages.title: Comparative advantage: diagrams, specialisation and limits
stages.sub: After this stage you can read gains from trade off a PPF, explain why specialisation raises output and choice, and judge the theory's assumptions and limits.

steps.q: You've drawn a country's PPF for cloth and wheat. Before any trade happens, where must the country actually be consuming?
steps.right: Somewhere on or inside its own PPF
steps.hint: Without trade, a country can only consume what it itself can produce.

steps.q: The country now specialises in the good it has a comparative advantage in, and trades for the other good. Can its new consumption bundle lie beyond its own PPF?
steps.right: Yes, trade lets it consume beyond its own PPF
steps.wrong: No, it is still stuck on its own PPF
steps.hint: Trade lets it swap surplus output for more of the other good than it could make itself.

steps.q: Comparing the pre-trade point on the PPF with the post-trade point beyond it, what has trade done for the country?
steps.right: Let it consume more of both goods than before
steps.wrong: Only changed which good it produces
steps.hint: Look at the two points: is the second one further out in both directions?

steps.q: Two countries each stop trying to make both goods and instead each focus on the good they're relatively best at. What happens to total combined output of both goods?

steps.q: With countries specialising and trading, shoppers can now buy goods made both at home and abroad, from many more producers competing for their custom. What tends to happen to the range of goods available and their prices?
steps.hint: More producers competing to sell into the same market: what does competition usually do to price and choice?

steps.q: You worked out comparative advantage earlier by comparing opportunity costs between two countries and two goods. For that calculation to hold up in the real world, what would need to be true — that costs stay constant and resources move freely, or that governments carefully manage the trade?
steps.right: Costs stay constant and resources move freely between goods
steps.wrong: Governments carefully manage which goods are traded
steps.hint: The calculation assumed simple, fixed conditions with nothing else interfering.

steps.q: In reality, transport costs exist, resources can't always switch easily between industries, and governments impose tariffs. Does the simple theory still predict trade patterns perfectly?
steps.right: No, real-world factors weaken its predictions
steps.wrong: Yes, it still holds exactly as calculated
steps.hint: Think about all the things assumed away that actually exist in real markets.
